site_article.answer_summary: Sign in to Dream Machine, upload a photo as the start frame (or type a prompt), turn on Draft mode to get quick previews, then upgrade the clip you like to full quality. Luma's price list charges Ray3.14 clips by length and resolution, for example 100 credits for 5 seconds at 720p.
site_article.hero_alt: Header image from Luma AI's Ray3 user guide for Dream Machine.

paragraphs.text: Dream Machine is Luma AI's app for making videos and images with AI. Its own video models are the Ray3 family, which can turn a text prompt or a still image into a short clip. If you want to know how to use Luma AI Dream Machine without burning through credits, the short version is: start from a photo, test in Draft mode, and only pay for full quality on the clip you keep.

Luma's current price list also offers other companies' models inside the same app, including Veo 3.1, Kling and Seedance for video and several image models, all paid from the same credit balance. This guide sticks to Luma's own Ray models, because that is what Dream Machine was built around.
How to use Luma AI Dream Machine, step by step

paragraphs.title: 1. Pick text or a photo
paragraphs.text: You can start from a text prompt (text to video) or from an image (image to video). Luma's Ray3 FAQ says the model does best with image to video, so if you have a good photo, start there. You get more control over how the first frame looks, and fewer wasted tries.

paragraphs.title: 2. Set keyframes
paragraphs.text: In the Keyframes tab you can set a start frame, an end frame or both, and Dream Machine fills in the motion between them. Each frame can be uploaded or made in Dream Machine first. Add a short prompt for the change you want; Luma's own example is a transition from sunset to a starry night.

paragraphs.title: 3. Turn on Draft mode
paragraphs.text: Switch on the Draft toggle in the composer window. Luma's Ray3 guide says drafts come back up to 5x faster, and its price list charges much less for draft generations. Use drafts to try different prompts and camera moves.

paragraphs.title: 4. Upgrade the one you like
paragraphs.text: When a draft looks right, upgrade it to the full quality version, which Luma calls Hi-Fi. According to Luma's prompting guide, the same prompt style works in both, so you do not need to rewrite anything.

paragraphs.title: 5. Choose HDR only if you need it
paragraphs.text: HDR is not switched on by default: you select it in the Dynamic Range dropdown in the settings panel. Luma's Ray3 FAQ says HDR and EXR downloads are limited to 540p and 720p and cost more credits, so leave it off unless you are grading the footage in a video editor.
Luma's FAQ suggests generating at 720p and upscaling afterward if you need a bigger file, instead of paying for a higher resolution on every try.
How to write a Ray3 prompt

Luma's help center recommends writing prompts like stage directions for a film, in a set order: the camera and its movement, the subject and the action, the setting, how materials and physics behave, the lighting and mood, and finally the style. It says physics only shows up reliably when you describe it, for example fabric that drapes with weight, and that words like slowly, rapidly or gently control the pace. The Ray3 FAQ adds that clear prompts of two to four sentences work best.

paragraphs.title: Prompt: A clip from a product photo
paragraphs.text: Slow push-in movement toward the [product] on a wooden table. Steam rises gently from the cup beside it. Soft morning light comes through a window on the left. Calm, realistic commercial style.

paragraphs.title: Prompt: A locked camera scene
paragraphs.text: Fixed viewpoint with no camera movement. A [person or animal] walks slowly across a [place] from left to right. Wind moves the grass and their clothes. Golden hour light, natural colors.

Everything in Dream Machine costs credits. On Luma's current price list, a Ray3.14 text or image to video clip costs 20 credits for 5 seconds at 360p, 100 credits at 720p and 400 credits at 1080p; a 10 second clip at 720p costs 300 credits. Luma's credit page says usage rounds up, so a 9 second clip is billed as 10 seconds.

Luma's pricing page lists three individual plans. Plus costs $30 a month, or $25 a month billed yearly, with 10,000 credits and commercial use. Pro costs $90 a month with 40,000 credits, and Ultra costs $300 a month with 150,000 credits. Monthly credits do not roll over. On a paid plan you can buy top up credits, starting at $4 for 1,200 credits, which last 12 months.

Luma's subscription page describes a free tier limited to Photon images and draft resolution Ray3.14 video, with watermarks and for personal projects only. Luma's help center says videos made on the Free and Lite tiers carry a watermark, and that a clip made before upgrading stays watermarked; you have to generate it again to get a clean copy. Dream Machine credits and Luma's developer API are billed separately.
To cancel, open your profile panel and choose Manage Subscription. Luma says you keep access until the end of the billing period, and that refund requests within 30 days go to its support email.

What it is bad at: Luma's own Ray3 FAQ says character consistency can vary, including shifts in a person's apparent age or gender between shots, and that extended, looped or keyframed clips sometimes have abrupt transitions. The same FAQ says Ray3 does not make sound, so plan to add audio in an editor. Clips are short, five to ten seconds per generation in that FAQ, so longer videos mean extending or stitching several shots. Check the credit cost on screen before every Hi-Fi generation, because prices differ a lot by model and resolution.
